title: The Machine That Changed the World
author: James P. Womack, Daniel T. Jones and Daniel Roos
theme: Lean production, pioneered by Toyota, does more with less than mass production and is set to replace it across industry.
summary: This book grew out of a five-year research programme at MIT that studied car makers around the world. Its authors set out to explain why some Japanese firms, above all Toyota, were building better cars with far fewer resources than their American and European rivals. Their answer was a new way of organising work, which they named lean production.

The authors frame the story as three eras. Craft production used skilled workers and simple tools to make a few expensive, varied vehicles. Henry Ford's mass production brought interchangeable parts, the moving assembly line and narrow, repetitive jobs, making cars cheap but rigid, with large inventories, armies of inspectors and rework at the end of the line. Lean production, developed at Toyota after the war, combines the strengths of both.

Comparing assembly plants, the researchers found that lean plants needed roughly half the labour hours, space and inventory of mass producers while making fewer defects. The differences come from practice, not automation. Workers operate in multi-skilled teams, are trusted to stop the line when they spot a problem and help fix its root cause. Parts arrive just in time, so stocks stay small and errors surface quickly. Machines are changed over fast, allowing small batches and wide variety.

The lean approach reaches beyond the factory. New models are designed by cross-functional teams under a strong project leader, cutting development time. Suppliers are treated as long-term partners who share cost and quality data instead of being played off against one another. Dealers keep close, lasting contact with customers.

The authors argue that lean production is not tied to Japanese culture, pointing to Japanese-run plants in North America that achieved similar results with local workers. Their conclusion is that every manufacturer, in cars and beyond, will need to adopt lean principles or fall behind.
takeaway: Eliminate waste, empower teams to fix problems at the source, and partner closely with suppliers and customers to do more with less.

questions.q: What research effort produced the findings in this book?
options: A government inquiry into Detroit
A multi-year MIT study of the world car industry
Toyota's internal training programme
A survey of European business schools
questions.why: The book reports the results of MIT's five-year international study of automobile manufacturing.

questions.q: Which term did the book popularise for Toyota's system?
options: Total quality management
Agile manufacturing
Lean production
Business process reengineering
questions.why: The authors named Toyota's approach lean production because it uses less of everything.

questions.q: Which three eras of production does the book describe?
options: Craft, mass and lean
Manual, mechanical and digital
Local, national and global
Agrarian, industrial and service
questions.why: The book traces the shift from craft production to mass production and then to lean production.

questions.q: What was a key weakness of mass production as the authors describe it?
options: Cars were too expensive for ordinary buyers
It relied on large inventories, narrow jobs and fixing defects late
It could not use moving assembly lines
It needed highly skilled craftsmen at every station
questions.why: Mass production made cars cheap but was rigid, with buffers of stock, repetitive jobs and rework at the end of the line.

questions.q: Roughly how did lean assembly plants compare with mass-production plants?
options: They used about twice the labour but fewer robots
They matched labour but used more space
They used about half the effort and space with fewer defects
They were cheaper only because of lower wages
questions.why: The study found lean plants needed about half the hours, space and inventory while producing higher quality.

questions.q: What may workers in a lean plant do when they see a problem?
options: Log it for the quality department to inspect later
Ignore it to keep the line moving
Send the car to a rework area
Stop the line and help solve the root cause
questions.why: Lean production trusts workers to halt the line so problems are fixed at the source rather than passed downstream.

questions.q: What is the purpose of just-in-time parts delivery?
options: To keep stocks small and expose errors quickly
To guarantee bulk discounts from suppliers
To allow longer production runs of one model
To replace the need for teamwork
questions.why: Small, timely deliveries reduce inventory and make defects visible before many bad parts pile up.

questions.q: How does lean product development differ from the traditional approach?
options: Each department works in sequence with little contact
Design is outsourced entirely to suppliers
Cross-functional teams work under a strong project leader
New models are only updated every twenty years
questions.why: A strong leader heading an integrated team shortens development time and reduces late changes.

questions.q: How do lean firms treat their suppliers?
options: As interchangeable vendors chosen on lowest bid each year
As long-term partners sharing cost and quality information
As competitors to be kept in the dark
As divisions to be fully owned and controlled
questions.why: Lean producers build lasting, cooperative relationships with suppliers rather than playing them off against each other.

questions.q: What evidence do the authors give that lean production is not bound to Japanese culture?
options: European craft workshops already used it
American unions designed the system
It worked only in plants inside Japan
Japanese-run plants in North America achieved similar results with local workers
questions.why: Transplant factories staffed by local workers matched much of the Japanese performance, showing the methods can travel.
